highlight.text: To this circumstance is probably due the increase in the number of the separate portraits of Persians other than those of members of the royal family-such as nobles, military officers, physicians, scholars, &c. — and the facile brush of Riza ‘Abbasi … was fortunately ready to supply [the] demand.

work.text: The primary colours and virtuoso technique of his early portraits give way in the 1620s to darker, earthier colours and a coarser, heavier line. New subjects only partly compensate for this disappointing stylistic development

source.author: Sheila R. Canby
source.title: Riza, in Grove Art Online (quoted in Wikipedia, “Reza Abbasi”)

work.text: He painted many older men, perhaps scholars, Sufi divines, or shepherds, as well as birds and Europeans, and in his last years sometimes satirized his subjects.

moment.text: They are decidedly mannered; a large number of them are single portraits of middle-aged men with curious long noses
moment.lead: Binyon, Wilkinson and Gray, on the many drawings signed Riza-yi ‘Abbasi:

source.author: Laurence Binyon, J. V. S. Wilkinson and Basil Gray
source.title: Persian Miniature Painting

moment.text: he is revealed as a born draughtsman of marked originality and a new realistic power, whose ingenious pencil delighted in seizing on the types of common people whom he met on his walks, and recording them in rapid [economical] strokes.

source.author: Laurence Binyon, J. V. S. Wilkinson and Basil Gray
source.title: Persian Miniature Painting

matters.text: His wild life is reflected in the kind of subjects that Riza ‘Abbasi so frequently chooses.
Riza ‘Abbasi, at his best, was brilliant at capturing personality in quick sketches.

source.author: Norah M. Titley
source.title: Persian Miniature Painting and its Influence on the Art of Turkey and India
